strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea of leveraging pretrained multi-view diffusion models both as a 2D→3D feature extractor and as a source of synthetic multi-view supervision, enabling training from single-view image collections without cameras, multi-view capture, or manual 3D annotations — a genuinely underexplored problem.

Demonstrates broad qualitative generalization across humans, dogs, and out-of-domain animal species (giraffe, rhino, horse, zebra) as well as non-human GSO objects, despite training on a single category/dataset, which is a compelling practical benefit.

The pipeline for turning predicted keypoints/edge graphs into an animatable rig (via MST extraction and Gaussian-based skinning) for 3D objects reconstructed from diffusion-generated views is a useful downstream application that showcases the alignment between predicted structure and the underlying 3D generative model's coordinate frame.

Ablations (diffusion features vs. ResNet features, number of virtual viewpoints) support the core claim that diffusion-derived multi-view features carry useful geometric priors beyond what a standard feature extractor obtains from the same generated images.
Clear presentation of the technical pipeline (feature aggregation, 3D unprojection, integral regression, multi-view reconstruction loss) with reasonably detailed equations.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is essentially limited to Human3.6M; despite substantial emphasis on animal/cross-species generalization (Stanford Dogs, AP-10K, GSO, DAVIS), no quantitative metrics (e.g., PCK, regression error against any pseudo/partial ground truth) are reported for these settings, so the strong generalization claims rest solely on qualitative figures.

On Human3.6M, the reported gains over the closest single-view baseline (Honari et al. [11], single-view) are modest and inconsistent across configurations (e.g., 130.58 vs 125.73 MPJPE with Linear regression for the 32-keypoint models is actually worse for some settings), weakening the claim of clearly outperforming prior single-view unsupervised methods.

The method still requires a fixed target camera-parameter set for the multi-view diffusion model to generate novel views; the paper does not clearly explain how these camera poses are chosen/fixed across training and whether this constitutes implicit camera information that is not truly 'camera-free,' which could be seen as tempering the 'no camera parameters' claim.

Computational cost is not quantified: iterative denoising to extract intermediate features plus generation of K views for both training and inference presumably incurs substantial runtime/memory overhead relative to feed-forward baselines, but no timing/throughput comparison is provided, limiting assessment of practicality.

Ablation study in the main text is narrow (only two axes: feature source and number of views), with more comprehensive ablations deferred to (unseen) supplementary material, making it hard to fully judge sensitivity to design choices such as timestep τ, grid resolution M, or number of keypoints N.

No failure-case analysis beyond a brief qualitative limitations paragraph; given the reliance on the diffusion model's generation quality, a more systematic study of failure modes (e.g., under strong articulation, occlusion, or unusual object shapes) would strengthen the paper's claims of robustness.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: code is promised but not yet released, and some architectural specifics (e.g., exact configuration of ϕ_kp, ϕ_vol, and the reconstruction network) are not fully detailed in the main paper.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: leveraging a pretrained multi-view diffusion model (SV3D) both as a source of synthetic multi-view supervision and as a geometry-aware feature extractor for unsupervised monocular 3D keypoint discovery, removing the need for calibrated multi-view capture or 3D annotations.

Technically sound pipeline: diffusion feature aggregation across layers, unprojection into a 3D volumetric representation, differentiable integral regression for keypoint localization, and a multi-view reconstruction loss with edge-map structural cues form a coherent, end-to-end differentiable system.

Strong empirical support: quantitative results on Human3.6M (competitive with/better than several multi-view and monocular baselines using only a single view), CUB-200-2011 2D projections, and qualitative results on Stanford Dogs, DAVIS, GSO, and AP-10K demonstrate good cross-category and out-of-domain generalization.

Extensive and informative ablations (Table 3 and supplementary Table 5) covering backbone choice, 3D lifting strategy, number of virtual viewpoints, keypoint count, diffusion timestep, data quantity, affine augmentation, view misalignment robustness, and aggregation strategy, which substantiate individual design choices.
Useful downstream application (animatable 3D object generation with skinning weights derived from predicted keypoints/edges) that showcases practical value beyond keypoint accuracy alone.

Reasonably transparent reporting of failure cases (left-right ambiguity, dependency on diffusion model quality) and honest discussion of reproducibility issues in baseline comparisons (CUB baseline reproduction appendix), which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Reliance on a single multi-view diffusion backbone (SV3D) raises questions about generality of the claims; the method's accuracy is explicitly coupled to the diffusion model's generation quality, as acknowledged in the failure case discussion, but no experiments with alternative multi-view diffusion backbones are shown in the main paper.

Quantitative comparison on CUB and Stanford Dogs is limited to projected 2D metrics rather than true 3D evaluation, since no 3D ground truth exists for these datasets; the paper explicitly states these 2D projections 'do not fully reflect the strengths of 3D predictions,' leaving the core 3D claims for non-human categories only qualitatively supported.

The number of keypoints (N=18) and their semantic identity are not consistently interpretable or validated against a canonical keypoint definition, and no quantitative keypoint correspondence/consistency metric (e.g., PCK across identity or cross-instance semantic consistency) is reported for animal categories.

Computational overhead is significant (diffusion generation and feature extraction), which is acknowledged (Table 6) but limits the immediate practicality of the method compared to lightweight baselines, and the trade-off is not deeply analyzed against accuracy gains.

Ablation and main experiments are conducted only on Human3.6M for quantitative studies; broader quantitative ablation on animal datasets is missing, so the generalization advantages claimed for CUB/Stanford Dogs rest mainly on qualitative figures.
The left-right ambiguity failure mode is a fairly fundamental limitation of the self-supervised formulation and is not addressed with any mitigation strategy, only reported as a known issue.

Some technical details (e.g., exact choice/justification of the aggregation weights, robustness of the Minimum Spanning Tree skeleton extraction for non-tree biological structures, sensitivity to keypoint count across categories) could be elaborated further for full reproducibility.
